2026 • تحديث : 27 أكتوبر 2026 SUDAN الخرطوم / عادل عبد الرحيم / الأناضول انقطع التيار الكهربائي عن أجزاء واسعة من الخرطوم، الثلاثاء، إثر استهداف طائرة مسيرة محطة المرخيات التحويلية للكهرباء في مدينة أم درمان غربي العاصمة السودانية. وأفاد شهود للأناضول بأن طائرة مسيرة هاجمت فجر الثلاثاء، محطة المرخيات شمال غربي أم درمان، ما أدى إلى انقطاع الكهرباء عن مناطق واسعة من الخرطوم. وأكد شهود من عدة أحياء بالعاصمة انقطاع التيار الكهربائي في مناطقهم صباحا. كما تداول ناشطون على مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي مقاطع مصورة تُظهر تصاعد الدخان من محطة المرخيات للكهرباء. وحتى الساعة 06:30 (ت.غ)، لم يصدر تعليق رسمي بشأن حجم الأضرار أو الجهة المسؤولة عن استهداف المحطة. ويأتي الهجوم غداة إعلان شركة كهرباء السودان أن "قوات الدعم السريع" استهدفت بطائرات مسيرة 5 محطات تحويلية للكهرباء في ولايات سنار (جنوب شرق) والقضارف (شرق) والجزيرة (وسط). وقالت الشركة الحكومية إن الهجمات ألحقت أضرارا بالغة بالمحطات، ما أدى إلى انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن الولايات الثلاث، إضافة إلى ولاية النيل الأبيض وسط البلاد. وتتهم السلطات السودانية ومنظمات وهيئات حقوقية قوات الدعم السريع باستهداف منشآت مدنية، فيما لا تعلق الأخيرة عادة على هذه الاتهامات، وتقول إنها تعمل على "حماية المدنيين". ومنذ أبريل/ نيسان 2023 يخوض الجيش السوداني و"الدعم السريع" حربا إثر خلافات بشأن تنظيم المؤسسة العسكرية، خلفت عشرات آلاف القتلى ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص، وتفاقم المجاعة والأزمة الإنسانية في البلاد. news_share news_share_description العوائق أمام المساعدات الإنسانية، محذرة من تدهور مقلق في الأمن الغذائي وخطر حدوث مجاعة خلال الأشهر المقبلة، في وقت أكدت فيه الحكومة السودانية أن الوضع الغذائي في البلاد مطمئن. وجاء في بيان مشترك نشرته وزارة الخارجية الأمريكية أن "السودان يشهد تدهورا مقلقا في أمنه الغذائي"، مضيفا أن "خطر المجاعة خلال الأشهر المقبلة، الذي حذرت منه مبادرة التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي ، يتطلب تحركا عاجلا". قصص مقترحة list of 2 items list 1 of 2 من خيام النزوح في دارفور.. مطالب إلى البرهان وترمب list 2 of 2 في الذكرى الأولى لمأساة الفاشر.. تحذيرات دولية من تجدد جرائم الإبادة في السودان end of list وأشار البيان إلى أن عدد من يعانون من انعدام الأمن الغذائي الحاد يُقدر بنحو 19.5 مليون شخص، أي 41% من سكان البلاد، في حين يواجه 5 ملايين شخص مستويات طارئة من انعدام الأمن الغذائي. وحذر من أن عدد الأطفال الذين يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم قد يتجاوز 825 ألف طفل ما لم تُتخذ إجراءات فورية لعكس هذا المسار. وأكد البيان أن "طرفي النزاع يتحملان المسؤولية الرئيسية عن تخفيف معاناة الشعب السوداني"، داعيا إياهما إلى السماح بالعمليات الإنسانية عبر جميع المسارات العابرة لخطوط القتال والحدود، بما في ذلك الوصول الجوي إلى إقليم دارفور غربي البلاد. كما دعا إلى ضمان استمرار وجود العاملين في المجال الإنساني وحمايتهم في أنحاء السودان وعدم شن هجمات على البنية التحتية المدنية. وفي ظل احتمال حدوث مجاعة، دعت الدول الموقعة على البيان المجتمع الدولي إلى زيادة التمويل، وحثت المؤسسات المالية على تكييف برامجها بما يتناسب مع وضع الأمن الغذائي في السودان. ووقعت على البيان حكومات 32 دولة، من بينها الولايات المتحدة وأستراليا وبريطانيا وفرنسا وألمانيا، إلى جانب المفوضة الأوروبية للمساواة والاستعداد وإدارة الأزمات. الحكومة تطمئن من جهتها، أكدت وزارة الخارجية السودانية أن الوضع الغذائي في البلاد مطمئن، وأن المخزون الإستراتيجي والعمليات الزراعية الجارية سيوفران الاحتياجات الغذائية، بما يدحض ما وصفته بمزاعم حدوث مجاعة. إعلان وقالت الخارجية السودانية إن البلاد لم تشهد مجاعة رغم استمرار الحرب ونهب مخزونها الاستراتيجي وتدمير بنتيها الأساسية، مرحبة بالدعم الإنساني المقدم من المانحين والمنظمات الدولية. وأوضحت أنها بدأت اتخاذ التدابير اللازمة لسد الفجوات الغذائية في المناطق المتأثرة بشح الأمطار والتصحر والنزوح القسري من مناطق الزراعة. وأكدت مواصلة تسهيل وصول المساعدات الإنسانية إلى جميع السودانيين، بما في ذلك المناطق الخاضعة لسيطرة "مليشيا الدعم السريع"، إلى جانب تيسير إصدار التأشيرات وأذونات الحركة للعاملين في المجال الإنساني. كما شددت على رفض استغلال المساعدات الإنسانية "غطاء لتمويل المليشيا وتقويتها"، واستخدام الغذاء سلاحا في الحرب ضد المدنيين، على حد تعبيرها. وأعربت الخارجية السودانية عن أسفها لما وصفته بمحاولات بعض الدول والمنظمات توظيف الأوضاع الإنسانية سياسيا، بهدف فرض شروط للتسوية تحت مسمى الهدنة الإنسانية. واعتبرت أن الهدنة الإنسانية المطروحة تستهدف إنقاذ من وصفتها بـ"المليشيا المتمردة" من الهزائم، ومنحها فرصة لإعادة التسلح والانتشار. واتهمت بعض الدول الغربية بتبني "مشروع سياسي يحمي المليشيا من مزيد من الهزائم، ويدفع نحو إجراء مفاوضات في ظل استمرار سيطرتها على أراض، خلافا لمرجعية إعلان جدة". وجددت الخارجية السودانية التزامها بالتعاون مع المنظمات الإنسانية، مؤكدة رفضها تسييس الأوضاع الإنسانية لخدمة أجندات تتعارض مع مصالح الشعب السوداني. الحرب وتداعياتها الإنسانية وفي يونيو/حزيران الماضي، قالت مبادرة التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي، وهي جهة عالمية لرصد الجوع مدعومة من الأمم المتحدة ، إن 5.1 ملايين شخص في السودان يواجهون جوعا حادا. ويواجه المزارعون صعوبات في جني محاصيلهم منذ اندلاع الحرب عام 2023، كما واجهوا موجة جفاف في الآونة الأخيرة. ويخوض الجيش السوداني قتالا ضد قوات الدعم السريع منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، بعد خلافات بين الطرفين بشأن قضايا من بينها كيفية دمج قواتهما في إطار انتقال مزمع إلى حكم مدني. وأدت الحرب إلى نزوح أكثر من 14 مليون شخص، وشهدت البلاد موجات من أعمال القتل بدوافع عرقية، وفقا لوكالة رويترز. وفي يوليو/تموز الماضي، خلص تحقيق أجرته الأمم المتحدة إلى أن قوات الدعم السريع نفذت عمليات قتل جماعي واغتصاب وتجويع قسري في مدينة حاصرتها وسيطرت عليها العام الماضي، في إطار سياسة متعمدة ترقى إلى مستوى الإبادة الجماعية . كما اتهمت واشنطن قوات الدعم السريع بارتكاب إبادة جماعية، والجيش السوداني بارتكاب جرائم حرب، وهو ما نفاه الطرفان. والشهر الماضي، قالت وزارة الخارجية الأمريكية إنه "لا القوات المسلحة السودانية ولا قوات الدعم السريع (شبه العسكرية) ولا أي من قادتهما يمثل حكما شرعيا ودستوريا للسودان". المصدر: الجزيرة + رويترز aj-logo aj-logo واجهوا موجة جفاف في الآونة الأخيرة. وحث البيان المشترك طرفي النزاع على السماح بالعمليات الإنسانية عبر كل المسارات العابرة لخطوط القتال والحدود، بما في ذلك الوصول الجوي إلى إقليم دارفور. كما دعا البيان من قادتهما "يمثلون حكما شرعيا ودستوريا للسودان". وأدت الحرب إلى نزوح أكثر من 14 مليون شخص، وأطلقت موجات من أعمال القتل ذات دوافع عرقية. وخلص تحقيق أجرته الأمم المتحدة في تموز، إلى أن قوات الدعم السريع وكشفت المصادر أن المقترح الأميركي لا يتضمن تفاصيل تتعلق بانسحاب القوات أو مواقع انتشارها، كما يخلو من آليات واضحة لمراقبة الهدنة وضمان الالتزام بوقف إطلاق النار. وأضافت المصادر أن مبعوث الرئيس الأميركي للشؤون العربية والأفريقية مسعد بولس طرح المبادرة بهدف اختبار فرص نجاح هدنة إنسانية، تمهيداً للانتقال إلى مراحل لاحقة من الجهود الرامية إلى إنهاء الحرب والتوصل إلى ترتيبات أكثر استدامة. وقال مصدر حكومي لـ"الشرق" إن الحكومة السودانية منفتحة على التعاطي بإيجابية مع أي مقترح للسلام تقدمه أي جهة، لكنه أكد أن نجاح أي مبادرة يقتضي معالجة قضايا أساسية، من بينها حماية المدنيين، ووقف تدفق السلاح، وإنهاء وجود قوات الدعم السريع في المناطق المدنية، ضمن إطار متكامل لإنهاء الحرب. اقرأ أيضاً اقرأ أيضاً بولس: الرباعية تتفق على حشد نفوذها لإنهاء حرب السودان عبر تسوية تفاوضية أعلن كبير مستشاري الرئيس الأميركي للشؤون العربية والإفريقية، مسعد بولس، أن دول الآلية الرباعية المعنية بالسودان اتفقت على توظيف قنوات اتصالها للتوصل إلى تسوية. وأضاف المصدر أن النقاش لا يتعلق بطول الفترة الزمنية للهدنة بقدر ما يرتبط بترتيباتها الميدانية وآليات تنفيذها وما يمكن أن تحققه على الأرض، معتبراً أن هذه الجوانب تمثل المعيار الأساسي للحكم على أي مبادرة مطروحة. واتهم المصدر مبعوث الرئيس الأميركي دونالد ترمب بـ"عدم الاهتمام بوقف الحرب والاستجابة لاحتياجات السودانيين وحماية المدنيين"، و"السعي فقط إلى تحقيق مكاسب سياسية قبل انتخابات التجديد النصفي للكونجرس الأميركي"، بحسب تعبيره. ويأتي المقترح الأميركي في وقت تشهد فيه الاتصالات الدبلوماسية المتعلقة بالملف السوداني حراكاً متجدداً، بعد تعثر جولات متعددة من الوساطات الإقليمية والدولية الساعية إلى وقف القتال بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع. أمين الجامعة العربية في الخرطوم من ناحية أخرى، بحث رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي السوداني عبد الفتاح البرهان، الاثنين، مع الأمين العام لجامعة الدول العربية نبيل فهمي، بالقصر الجمهوري في الخرطوم، تطورات الأوضاع في السودان والجهود الرامية إلى تحقيق السلام والاستقرار في البلاد. كما التقى فهمي رئيس الوزراء السوداني كامل إدريس، وتناول معه سبل دعم جهود السلام في السودان ومسار الحوار الوطني، إلى جانب المبادرة السودانية المقدمة إلى مجلس الأمن في ديسمبر 2025. وجدد الأمين العام الترحيب الذي سبق أن أعربت عنه جامعة الدول العربية بهذه المبادرة، مؤكداً أهمية البناء عليها في إطار الجهود الرامية إلى إنهاء الحرب ومعالجة الأزمة السودانية، وتعزيز فرص التوصل إلى تسوية سياسية شاملة بقيادة وملكية سودانية. وقال فهمي، في تصريحات صحفية عقب اللقاء، إن السودان يحظى بأهمية خاصة في محيطه العربي، مشيراً إلى الدور الذي اضطلع به تاريخياً في دعم القضايا العربية، ومؤكداً التزام جامعة الدول العربية بدعم سيادة السودان ووحدة أراضيه ومساندة مؤسساته الوطنية. وأضاف أن زيارته تأتي في إطار اهتمام الدول العربية بالقضية السودانية وحرصها على المساهمة في معالجة تداعيات الأزمة، لافتاً إلى أن قرارات المجالس الوزارية العربية والقمم العربية ركزت على دعم جهود إحلال السلام والاستقرار في السودان والمساهمة في مرحلة إعادة الإعمار. وأوضح الأمين العام لجامعة الدول العربية أنه سيواصل لقاءاته مع المسؤولين السودانيين، إلى جانب لجنة تهيئة الحوار السوداني، للاستماع إلى رؤاهم بشأن سبل إنهاء الأزمة وإرساء السلام واستعادة الاستقرار في البلاد. وتتركز المشاورات الدولية والإقليمية الجارية على التوصل إلى هدنة إنسانية يمكن أن تمهد لوقف دائم لإطلاق النار، وتعزيز وصول المساعدات الإنسانية، وتهيئة مسار سياسي سوداني شامل يضع حداً للصراع المستمر منذ أبريل 2023. ومنذ اندلاع الحرب بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع، فشلت عدة اتفاقات لوقف إطلاق النار في الصمود، وسط تبادل الاتهامات بين طرفي النزاع بخرق التعهدات المعلنة، فيما تواصل المنظمات الدولية التحذير من تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية واتساع نطاق النزوح وانعدام الأمن الغذائي في مناطق واسعة من البلاد. تصنيفات سياسة الجامعة العربية عبد الفتاح البرهان السودان الشرق الأوسط غيتي أوضاع إنسانية صعبة يعيشها السودانيون في ظل الحرب - غيتي الخط تحذيرات دولية من تدهور الأمن الغذائي وخطر الجوع الحاد في السودان، وسط دعوات أميركية وأوروبية لتسهيل دخول المساعدات وحماية العاملين الإنسانيين. قالت عشرات الدول، من بينها الولايات المتحدة وقوى أوروبية كبرى، إن السودان يشهد تدهورًا مقلقًا في أمنه الغذائي، ودعت طرفي النزاع إلى "إزالة جميع العوائق أمام المساعدات الإنسانية". وأضافت الدول، في بيان مشترك، أنها تدعو المجتمع الدولي إلى زيادة التمويل، في ظل خطر حدوث مجاعة، كما تحث المؤسسات المالية على تكييف برامجها القائمة بما يتناسب مع وضع الأمن الغذائي في البلاد. تحذيرات من تفاقم الجوع في السودان وجاء في البيان، الذي نشرته وزارة الخارجية الأميركية : "يشهد السودان تدهورًا مقلقًا في أمنه الغذائي. إن خطر المجاعة خلال الأشهر المقبلة، الذي حذرت منه مبادرة التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي، يتطلب تحركًا عاجلًا". إقرأ أيضاً مجتمع - السودان الجفاف يهدد السودان بمجاعة جديدة.. تحذيرات من كارثة تفاقمها الحرب وأضاف البيان: "يتحمل طرفا النزاع المسؤولية الرئيسية عن تخفيف معاناة الشعب السوداني". ويخوض الجيش السوداني قتالًا ضد قوات الدعم السريع شبه العسكرية منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، بعدما اختلف الطرفان بشأن قضايا من بينها كيفية دمج قواتهما في إطار انتقال مزمع إلى حكم مدني. وفي يونيو/ حزيران، قالت مبادرة التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي، وهي جهة عالمية لرصد الجوع مدعومة من الأمم المتحدة، إن 5.1 ملايين شخص في السودان يواجهون جوعًا حادًا. ويكافح المزارعون لحصاد محاصيلهم منذ اندلاع الحرب عام 2023، كما واجهوا موجة جفاف في الآونة الأخيرة. وحث البيان المشترك طرفي النزاع على السماح بتنفيذ العمليات الإنسانية عبر جميع المسارات العابرة لخطوط القتال والحدود، بما في ذلك إتاحة الوصول الجوي إلى إقليم دارفور. كما دعا الطرفين إلى "ضمان استمرار وجود العاملين في المجال الإنساني وحمايتهم" في أنحاء السودان، والامتناع عن شن هجمات على البنية التحتية المدنية. المجاعة في السودان ودعوات لرفع القيود عن المساعدات أطلقت عشرات الدول، وفي مقدمتها الولايات المتحدة وقوى أوروبية كبرى، تحذيرات شديدة اللهجة من التدهور المتسارع في حالة الأمن الغذائي داخل السودان. وأكدت هذه الدول في بيان مشترك أن البلاد تواجه خطراً حقيقياً يتمثل في وقوع مجاعة وشيكة خلال الأشهر المقبلة. وطالب البيان المجتمع الدولي بضرورة التحرك العاجل لتفادي كارثة إنسانية غير مسبوقة. دعت الدول الموقعة على البيان طرفي النزاع في السودان إلى إزالة كافة العوائق التي تحول دون وصول المساعدات الإنسانية إلى المتضررين. وشددت على ضرورة فتح المسارات العابرة لخطوط القتال والحدود بشكل كامل لضمان تدفق الإمدادات الغذائية والطبية. كما حثت المؤسسات المالية الدولية على تكييف برامجها التمويلية بما يتناسب مع خطورة الوضع الراهن في البلاد. أشارت مصادر دولية إلى أن مبادرة التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي قد حذرت مسبقاً من تفاقم أزمة الجوع. وأوضح البيان المشترك الذي نشرته الخارجية الأمريكية أن المسؤولية الرئيسية في تخفيف معاناة الشعب السوداني تقع على عاتق طرفي الصراع. ويأتي هذا التحذير في وقت يعاني فيه الملايين من نقص حاد في الاحتياجات الأساسية للبقاء على قيد الحياة. تؤكد التقارير الميدانية أن أكثر من 5 ملايين شخص في السودان يواجهون حالياً مستويات حادة من الجوع تهدد حياتهم بشكل مباشر. وقد تسببت الحرب المستمرة منذ أبريل 2023 في شلل تام للقطاع الزراعي، حيث يعجز المزارعون عن حصاد محاصيلهم. وزاد من تعقيد المشهد موجة الجفاف التي ضربت عدة مناطق، مما أدى إلى انهيار الإنتاج المحلي للغذاء. طالب البيان المشترك بضرورة توفير الحماية الكاملة للعاملين في المجال الإنساني وضمان استمرار تواجدهم في كافة أنحاء السودان دون ترهيب. وشددت الدول الموقعة على تجريم الهجمات التي تستهدف البنية التحتية المدنية والمنشآت الحيوية. وأكدت أن استهداف الأعيان المدنية يفاقم من حدة الأزمة الإنسانية ويعطل جهود الإغاثة الدولية. شملت قائمة الدول الموقعة على البيان التحذيري كلاً من الولايات المتحدة وبريطانيا وفرنسا وألمانيا وأستراليا، بالإضافة إلى المفوضية الأوروبية. وتعكس هذه المشاركة الواسعة حجم القلق الدولي تجاه المآلات الكارثية للصراع المسلح في السودان. ويهدف هذا التحرك الدبلوماسي إلى الضغط على الأطراف المتصارعة للالتزام بالقانون الدولي الإنساني. أفادت مصادر بأن تحقيقات أممية أجريت مؤخراً خلصت إلى ارتكاب قوات الدعم السريع لانتهاكات جسيمة شملت القتل الجماعي والتجويع القسري. وأشارت التحقيقات إلى أن هذه الممارسات، التي وقعت في مدن محاصرة العام الماضي، قد ترقى إلى مستوى الإبادة الجماعية. وتأتي هذه النتائج لتسلط الضوء على حجم المأساة التي يعيشها المدنيون في مناطق النزاع. من جانبها، أكدت واشنطن في تصريحات سابقة أن أياً من طرفي النزاع لا يمثل حكماً شرعياً أو دستورياً للشعب السوداني. واتهمت الإدارة الأمريكية قوات الدعم السريع بارتكاب أعمال إبادة، بينما وجهت اتهامات للجيش بارتكاب جرائم حرب. ورغم هذه الاتهامات، يستمر الطرفان في نفي ارتكاب أي انتهاكات ممنهجة ضد المدنيين. تسببت الحرب الأهلية المندلعة منذ أكثر من عام في نزوح ما يزيد عن 14 مليون سوداني بعيداً عن ديارهم. وأدت العمليات العسكرية إلى موجات نزوح داخلي وخارجي واسعة النطاق، مما خلق أزمة لاجئين هي الأكبر في المنطقة. وتترافق هذه التحركات السكانية مع تصاعد في أعمال القتل ذات الدوافع العرقية في عدة أقاليم. يعود أصل النزاع المسلح إلى خلافات حادة بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع حول خطط دمج القوات ضمن هيكل عسكري موحد. وكان من المفترض أن يمهد هذا الدمج الطريق لانتقال البلاد نحو حكم مدني ديمقراطي، إلا أن الصدام المسلح أجهض هذه التطلعات. ومنذ ذلك الحين، دخلت البلاد في نفق مظلم من العنف والدمار الاقتصادي. شددت الدول الكبرى على ضرورة تأمين الوصول الجوي للمساعدات، خاصة إلى إقليم دارفور الذي يعاني من حصار خانق. وأوضحت المصادر أن العوائق البيروقراطية والأمنية تمنع وصول القوافل الإغاثية إلى المناطق الأكثر احتياجاً. ويعد فتح الممرات الإنسانية مطلباً ملحاً لا يقبل التأجيل لإنقاذ آلاف الأرواح من الموت جوعاً. ختاماً، دعا البيان المشترك المجتمع الدولي إلى زيادة التمويل المخصص للاستجابة الإنسانية في السودان بشكل فوري. وأكدت الدول أن الفجوة التمويلية تعيق قدرة المنظمات الدولية على تقديم الوجبات الغذائية والرعاية الطبية. ويبقى الرهان حالياً على مدى استجابة الأطراف المتصارعة للضغوط الدولية لوقف إطلاق النار وتسهيل مهام الإغاثة. دلالات السودان مجاعة الأمم المتحدة مساعدات إنسانية الولايات المتحدة شارك برأيك أرسل جاري التحديث ethiopia.content: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: All of Africa Today - October 27, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 27 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda More Than 60 Killed In Attacks In Ethiopia More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks targeting Christian communities in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The attacks occurred in three areas of the Shirka district, where at least 20 houses were reportedly burnt down, and five children were among those killed. One resident described the violence as an ambush, saying attackers surrounded the community from all sides. A church official called the incident a massacre, adding that security forces arrived but were unable to stop the assault. Many residents have since fled the area. A local official blamed a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented on the latest allegations and previously denied responsibility for similar attacks. The Orthodox Church condemned the violence, saying attacks against Christians have increased and accusing authorities of failing to address repeated concerns about insecurity. A July 2026 report by the Ethiopian Human Rights Council recorded 458 deaths in attacks in the area over the previous four years, identifying local communities, particularly Orthodox Christians, as frequent targets. However, previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims, with residents describing the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature. Algeria Approves Troop Deployment To Niger Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Algeria is preparing to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger in its first foreign military deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. The proposed deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister as the country seeks assistance in combating armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria's parliament approved the deployment, with 148 of 174 senators voting in favour before the lower house also backed the move. Algeria has not yet announced the timing or number of troops, but they are expected to help secure energy infrastructure in northern Niger, near the Libyan border. The operation would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision permitting overseas military deployments and a significant departure from Algeria's longstanding opposition to sending troops abroad. Algerian officials have stressed that the mission is intended to protect economic infrastructure rather than wage war. The country has significant economic interests in Niger, including a proposed gas pipeline that would transport Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. UN Warns 3.6 Million in Uganda Facing Acute Food Insecurity as Crisis Worsens About 3.6 million people in Uganda face high levels of acute food insecurity, and the number is projected to rise to 4.4 million between February and June 2027, according to the 2026 Integrated Food Security Phase Classification report. Refugees and communities in the Karamoja sub-region are expected to face the greatest burden as food shortages and malnutrition worsen. The report estimates that 465,900 children under five and 246,300 pregnant and breastfeeding women will require treatment for acute malnutrition between April 2026 and March 2027. The crisis is being driven by recurring climate shocks, declining agricultural production, crop and livestock pests and diseases, high food prices, deteriorating livelihoods and limited access to healthcare, clean water, sanitation and social protection. United Nations Resident Coordinator in Uganda Leonard Zulu called for urgent action to protect vulnerable households and strengthen food systems before conditions deteriorate further. Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja urged the government, development partners and humanitarian agencies to invest in sustainable solutions that enable communities to produce their own food and reduce dependence on emergency assistance. The assessment, conducted across 60 districts between August and September 2026, was launched alongside a $50 million joint appeal by the United Nations and its partners to support emergency responses in Karamoja and early interventions in 37 districts and eight refugee settlements. The proposed response includes cash assistance, agricultural and livestock support, nutrition screening and treatment, healthcare, child protection, gender-based violence prevention, water and sanitation programmes, and disaster preparedness. The report warns that without sustained investment and coordinated action, vulnerable communities could face worsening hunger and malnutrition in the coming months. Amnesty Warns Funding Crisis Could Shut Central African Republic War Crimes Court Amnesty International has warned that suspected perpetrators of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic (CAR), including senior officials, could escape justice if the country's Special Criminal Court (SCC) fails to secure urgent funding. In a report released in October 2026, the organisation said the court, inaugurated in 2018, has tried six cases and secured convictions against 19 people for war crimes and crimes against humanity, with reparations awarded to victims in one case. However, many survivors of atrocities committed during the 2003 coup and the 2012–2014 armed conflict are still waiting for those responsible to be prosecuted. The United States withdrew its funding in 2025, leaving more than US$4.15 million in unpaid commitments and plunging the court into an unprecedented financial crisis. The United Nations and European Union are now its only financial contributors, while funding shortages have forced staff reductions, including cuts to the witness protection unit, and prevented prosecutors from opening new investigations. Amnesty warned that the court could close when its mandate expires in October 2028 unless additional funding is secured. Ukraine Allegedly Supporting Mali Militia Ukraine is facing questions over its alleged involvement in supporting Tuareg fighters in northern Mali, a development that could extend its rivalry with Russia into Africa's Sahel region. A September 2026 CNN investigation reported that around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists were assisting Tuareg fighters, although DW said it had not independently verified the claims and Ukraine has not confirmed a specific operation. Analysts believe any involvement would fit Kyiv's broader strategy of weakening Russian influence internationally, particularly in countries where Moscow provides military support to governments. Mali's military authorities have increasingly relied on Russia for security assistance since taking power in coups in 2020 and 2021, with Russia's Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group's role in 2025. The milestone highlights ongoing national efforts to streamline business procedures and expand online public services. The ministry's latest online services report reveals that 1,088,787 services were delivered across federal institutions, regional states, and city administrations, underscoring the expanding role of digital platforms in the country's commercial administration. Among the regions, Oromia Regional State recorded the highest volume with 441,550 services provided. Addis Ababa followed with 204,512, Amhara with 156,193, and South Ethiopia with 101,891. By service category, trade name clearance accounted for the largest share, with 579,785 services delivered. Business license renewals followed with 122,730, while license amendments totaled 107,317. New business registrations accounted for 60,409 services. The ministry said the digital system was helping reduce bureaucratic burdens on the business community while improving the efficiency, accessibility and transparency of public service delivery. The expansion of digital business registration and licensing services is part of Ethiopia's broader digital transformation agenda, which aims to modernize public administration, simplify procedures and improve access to government services through technology. ethiopia.content: Egypt to Deploy Troops in Somalia Under Bilateral Deal Ahead of Aussom Integration - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Egypt to Deploy Troops in Somalia Under Bilateral Deal Ahead of Aussom Integration 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Egypt is preparing to deploy troops to Somalia under a bilateral military cooperation agreement before transferring approximately 1,000 personnel into the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), raising concerns over operational coordination and command structures. According to The East African report on 25 October, the initial deployment is expected to comprise a brigade-sized battle group with support elements in Middle Shabelle, north of Mogadishu. A tactical headquarters is planned at Ceelcade, near Ciciley airfield, an area currently held by Burundian AU troops. Additional Egyptian forces could be stationed elsewhere at Somalia's request, although Cairo has not disclosed the full size of its deployment. The African Union has yet to publicly clarify how the bilateral force will coordinate with AUSSOM and other contingents. Burundi's troops, which receive logistical support through the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), have reportedly not been formally notified of the proposed arrangements and have indicated they will not operate under a bilateral command structure. They are prepared to withdraw once replaced. Egypt was allocated approximately 1,091 troops under AUSSOM in late 2024 but delayed formal participation, citing funding constraints. Deploying under a bilateral agreement before integration raises questions over command authority, accountability, logistics and potential operational overlap. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Egypt and Somalia signed a military cooperation agreement in August 2024, followed by Egyptian shipments of weapons, ammunition and armoured vehicles, as well as military training and advisory support. In August 2025, Somalia's Defence Ministry announced the completion of specialised training for Egyptian units intended for AUSSOM . A 16-member Egyptian military reconnaissance delegation visited Mogadishu the following month to assess deployment sites and logistics. Addis Standard previously reported o n preparations for the deployment , including troop movements and site work at Ceelcade, as formal integration remained delayed by funding and logistical challenges. The planned deployment comes as AUSSOM faces financial and operational pressures while supporting Somali forces against Al-Shabaab. Uncertainty over logistical support through UNSOS, amid questions about continued US funding, has further complicated the mission's sustainability. The move also carries regional implications amid longstanding tensions between Egypt and Ethiopia over the Nile waters and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), alongside competing interests in Red Sea access. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Calls for Hydro-Diplomacy On Shared Rivers As Egypt's El-Sisi Reiterates Water Security Is a 'Red Line'
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Calls for Hydro-Diplomacy On Shared Rivers As Egypt's El-Sisi Reiterates Water Security Is a 'Red Line' - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Calls for Hydro-Diplomacy On Shared Rivers As Egypt's El-Sisi Reiterates Water Security Is a 'Red Line' 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia has called for stronger regional cooperation and hydro-diplomacy over shared water resources, while Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi warned that Cairo would not accept any fait accompli that compromises its water security, highlighting the persistent divide between the two countries over the management of the Nile. The contrasting positions emerged as Ethiopia's third Water and Energy Week opened on 26 October and El-Sisi addressed the ninth Cairo Water Week a day earlier, with both countries emphasizing cooperation while maintaining their respective positions on the use and management of shared water resources. In a message delivered on behalf of Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Itefa, Ethiopia's Ministry of Water and Energy emphasized the need for constructive engagement, reliable information-sharing and practical cooperation among countries sharing rivers. According to ENA , the ministry described hydro-diplomacy as a pathway to regional integration and called for science-based policymaking to turn shared water challenges into opportunities for development and stability. The ministry also highlighted Ethiopia's water and renewable energy potential, stressing the importance of effective resource management, coordinated institutions and sustainable investment. It identified expanding access to affordable energy, improving water supply and sanitation, strengthening irrigation and water-use efficiency, and protecting groundwater and water-source catchments as key priorities. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines It further called for stronger hydrological and meteorological monitoring, improved basin information systems and greater collaboration among governments, researchers, investors and development partners to guide decisions on shared resources. Egypt reiterates water security concerns Speaking at the opening of Cairo Water Week on 25 October, El-Sisi said the Nile provides Egypt with more than 98% of its renewable water resources, making the river central to the country's water security. In his address, reported by Xinhua News Agency, the Egyptian president said Cairo respected the right of all Nile Basin countries to development and supported cooperation in energy, agriculture and irrigation. He expressed interest in strengthening cooperation in the Eastern Nile Basin, particularly among Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia. However, El-Sisi stressed that development must not come at the expense of another country's water security. "Any wager that Egypt will accept a fait accompli or compromise its water security is a losing wager," he said. He argued that prior notification, the exchange of studies and consultation were practical tools for building trust and protecting the interests of countries sharing water resources. He also reiterated Egypt's commitment to cooperation based on international law, coordination, good neighbourliness and the principle of causing no harm. The remarks reflect Cairo's longstanding concerns over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), which Ethiopia officially inaugurated in September 2025. Egypt and Sudan have repeatedly raised concerns about the dam's implications for downstream water security, while years of trilateral negotiations have failed to produce a binding agreement governing its filling and operation. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has maintained that the hydropower project is intended to expand electricity generation and support economic development without harming downstream countries. Cooperation remains untested Despite their differing emphases, both countries have presented cooperation as necessary for managing shared water resources. Ethiopia's latest statement focused on hydro-diplomacy, integrated planning and science-based decision-making, while El-Sisi stressed consultation and safeguards against actions that could threaten Egypt's water security. Their statements, however, do not indicate a breakthrough in the longstanding dispute over the GERD. The central challenge remains reconciling Ethiopia's development ambitions with Egypt's demand for assurances over the management of the Nile, alongside Sudan's interests as another downstream country. Ethiopia's Water and Energy Week, running from 26 to 30 October, is expected to produce policy recommendations, partnerships and investment proposals aimed at strengthening the water and energy sectors. Cairo Water Week, held under the theme "Water as a Catalyst for Peace, Shared Prosperity and a Sustainable Planet," is bringing together participants to discuss water security, capacity-building and preparations for the 2026 UN Water Conference, scheduled to take place in the United Arab Emirates in December. Whether these parallel calls for cooperation translate into progress on the GERD dispute will depend on the three countries' ability to bridge their differences through sustained negotiations, information-sharing and arrangements that address their competing interests in the Nile's use and management. ethiopia.title: Holy Synod Confirms 60 Orthodox Faithful Killed in Latest Attacks in Oromia, Calls for Protection, Justice
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Holy Synod Confirms 60 Orthodox Faithful Killed in Latest Attacks in Oromia, Calls for Protection, Justice - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Holy Synod Confirms 60 Orthodox Faithful Killed in Latest Attacks in Oromia, Calls for Protection, Justice 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod has confirmed that 60 Orthodox faithful were killed in attacks in two districts of Oromia's Arsi Zone on 20 and 24 October, while more than 20 others sustained severe injuries and 20 homes were burned down, according to a statement issued on Monday. The Holy Synod said 14 people were killed in Angada Kebele, specifically in Gora Silingo, Merti Woreda, on 20 October, while another 46 were killed in Tereta, Chole and Birbo in Shirka Woreda on 24 October . "We have heard with deep sorrow the report submitted by the Diocese Office," the Holy Synod said, describing the killings as "extremely tragic cruelty and suffering inflicted on our citizens." The statement, issued on 26 October, said the victims were innocent Orthodox faithful and warned that killings, displacement, physical harm and destruction of property targeting Orthodox Christians in Arsi and other parts of Ethiopia had continued to escalate. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Church strongly condemned the attacks, saying they violated the constitutional rights to life and freedom of religion and undermined Ethiopia's values of peaceful coexistence. "Since such an abject act is completely unacceptable under any religious teaching or human rights principles," the statement said, the Holy Synod considered the violence an act that "deserves outright condemnation." The Synod called on government institutions to publicly condemn the killings, protect civilians and ensure that those responsible were brought to justice. It urged relevant authorities to uphold the constitutional rights to life and freedom of worship and provide legal protection to prevent similar attacks. The Church also called on security agencies to give the affected communities special attention, provide protection until the security situation is resolved and take preventive measures against further violence. The latest attacks come amid a broader pattern of reported killings and displacement in East Arsi, where Orthodox Christian communities have repeatedly been targeted. In July 2026, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi since 2021/2022, documenting killings, kidnappings for ransom and forced displacement. Previous attacks in the zone have also involved the destruction and looting of churches and the killing of clergy and worshippers, prompting repeated appeals from religious leaders for investigations and accountability. ethiopia.title: From Strategic Asset to Regional Fault Line - Djibouti At Crossroads of Red Sea Power Struggle
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: From Strategic Asset to Regional Fault Line - Djibouti At Crossroads of Red Sea Power Struggle - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: From Strategic Asset to Regional Fault Line - Djibouti At Crossroads of Red Sea Power Struggle 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — For three decades, Djibouti's political economy rested on a simple model: Ethiopia needed Djibouti's ports, and Djibouti needed Ethiopia's trade. Around that relationship, President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh's government built a model based on ports, foreign military bases, strategic infrastructure, and external financing. That arrangement transformed one of Africa's smallest states into one of its most strategically important. However, the foundations beneath that model are shifting. The Red Sea security crisis, Houthi attacks around the Bab el-Mandeb, Ethiopia's search for alternative maritime access, growing competition around Berbera and Zeila, Djibouti's debt burden, a persistent Afar insurgency, staggering youth unemployment, and an unresolved succession question are no longer isolated problems. They are intersecting simultaneously across maritime corridors, borderlands, and domestic institutions. Djibouti is becoming a primary fault line in what increasingly resembles a Red Sea Cold War--a fluid regional competition involving Ethiopia, Somalia, Somaliland, Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel, China, the United States, and armed non-state actors. The irony is profound: for decades, Djibouti turned raw geography into political leverage, but today, that same geography risks turning into its greatest strategic vulnerability. Bab el-Mandeb under fire Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, represents one of the world's most vital maritime chokepoints. Djibouti sits directly beside it, a proximity that historically made the nation indispensable to global shipping and major military powers. However, the sustained Houthi campaign against commercial shipping has altered that strategic calculation. The United Nations Security Council has repeatedly condemned Houthi attacks on merchant vessels, while maritime authorities continue to warn commercial operators about severe operational risks in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Major shipping lines have rerouted vessels around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding weeks to journey times while increasing fuel consumption, war-risk insurance premiums, and pressure on global supply chains. The economic impact on Djibouti is nuanced. According to official country assessments by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Djibouti experienced strong growth driven by a seven point four percent increase in overall port activity and a ninety-eight percent surge in transshipment as operators adjusted to Red Sea disruptions. Yet, the IMF simultaneously warned that this temporary windfall should not be mistaken for structural security, noting that Djibouti remains vulnerable to regional shocks and medium-term competition from neighboring commercial ports. The primary long-term threat to Djibouti is not an immediate abandonment of its quays but a structural realignment where regional neighbors systematically develop alternative maritime routes. When dependence becomes leverage Djibouti's relationship with Ethiopia has always been mutually dependent, though asymmetric. Landlocked Ethiopia relies overwhelmingly on Djibouti for its international maritime trade, while Djibouti has constructed its state balance sheet around servicing the Ethiopian market. Roads, railways, customs systems, and container terminals have transformed the Addis Ababa-Djibouti corridor into the most critical economic artery in the Horn of Africa. The geography that made the nation powerful can no longer shield it from the consequences of a changing regional order." While this relationship remains indispensable, Ethiopia has made clear its intention to establish corridor redundancy. The January 2024 Memorandum of Understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland marked a major strategic shift, contemplating Ethiopian access to coastal territory in Somaliland for commercial and naval facilities. Although Somalia rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, the MoU demonstrated that Ethiopia no longer regards maritime access as an exclusive dependency on Djibouti. As highlighted in reporting on regional maritime developments by Addis Standard , the commercial expansion of Berbera presents a structural challenge for Djibouti. The IMF explicitly identified port competition in Somaliland, Eritrea, Kenya, and Sudan as a long-term risk capable of eroding Djibouti's market share of Ethiopian trade. Ethiopia does not need to abandon Djibouti entirely; it only needs alternative gateways to fundamentally alter its bargaining leverage. The price of strategic infrastructure Djibouti's transformation into a logistics hub required massive capital investment, financed heavily through Chinese state loans. According to the IMF's debt sustainability analysis , Djibouti's public debt-to-GDP ratio surged from thirty-four point nine percent in 2013 to nearly seventy percent, driven by megaprojects such as the electric Addis Ababa-Djibouti Railway, the Doraleh Multipurpose Port, the Port of Ghoubet, and the cross-border water pipeline. The IMF officially classifies Djibouti as being in debt distress, assessing its public debt as unsustainable. This highlights the structural vulnerability of Djibouti's model: capital-intensive infrastructure built against expectations of future trade revenues creates severe fiscal strain when external shocks intervene. Because Djibouti remains heavily dependent on Ethiopian economic growth, any slowdown in trade volume directly impairs the state's capacity to service its dollar-denominated obligations to Chinese lenders like the Export-Import Bank of China. Djibouti's strategic prominence is magnified by its extraordinary concentration of foreign military installations . The United States, France, China, Japan, and Italy maintain permanent bases across the country. American Camp Lemonnier serves as Washington's primary military hub in Africa, while Beijing's facility represents China's first overseas naval support base . This arrangement provides Djibouti with foreign exchange rental income and international security partnerships, but it also creates an operational paradox. The concentration of foreign military power makes Djibouti a prime target during regional escalations. Furthermore, as strategic competition between the United States and China intensifies globally, Djibouti remains one of the rare locations where their military assets operate in immediate physical proximity. FRUD and the Afar question External pressures are compounded by unresolved domestic grievances. The armed faction of the Front for the Restoration of Unity and Democracy, known as FRUD-Armée, continues its long-standing guerrilla opposition against the gover nment. Originating from historic Afar grievances regarding political and economic marginalization, FRUD fighters periodically attack military garrisons in the northern and western districts of Tadjoura, Obock, and Dikhil. Following an attack on a northern military post in October 2022 that resulted in troop casualties, the government formally designated FRUD-Armée as a terrorist organization. Security operations have increasingly incorporated air strikes and drone capabilities. In February 2025, Djiboutian authorities announced that a drone strike near Addorta, close to the Ethiopian border, killed eight insurgents, while acknowledging civilian casualties. Media reports noted disputes over whether the strike occurred on Djiboutian or Ethiopian soil, illustrating how domestic counter-insurgency operations can quickly evolve into cross-border diplomatic disputes. The FRUD insurgency is sustained by severe socio-economic conditions. Despite headline GDP growth generated by port services and base leases, economic benefits remain concentrated among a narrow political elite. According to labor assessments published by the World Bank , more than half of the working-age population remains outside the formal labor force. Data reveals an acute demographic crisis among the youth population. Youth unemployment for citizens aged fifteen to twenty-four reached approximately seventy-six point eight percent, while nearly forty-six percent of young people aged sixteen to twenty-four are classified as NEET--Not in Education, Employment, or Training. Furthermore, over sixty percent of private economic activity takes place in the informal sector, providing minimal wage security, and wealth inequality remains elevated, with over forty-two percent of the population living below the official poverty line. This economic exclusion operates alongside complete political closure. Following constitutional amendments that removed presidential age limits, President Guelleh secured a sixth term in the national election with ninety-seven point eight percent of the vote after main opposition parties boycotted the poll. For thousands of disenfranchised youth, the combination of economic marginalization and political exclusion makes armed rebellion an increasingly attractive alternative. The Afar community spans the contiguous borderlands of Djibouti, Ethiopia, and Eritrea, creating cross-border kinship networks that facilitate logistics and sanctuary. Historically, regional states have weaponized these networks; during the 1998-2000 Ethiopia-Eritrea war, both governments supported opposing Afar rebel movements to destabilize their rival. However, Ethiopia faces a clear strategic constraint regarding Djibouti. Because Addis Ababa relies on the Djibouti transport corridor for the vast majority of its commercial trade, it has no incentive to support an insurgency capable of destabilizing the Djiboutian state. The primary risk remains a persistent, low-level border insurgency where FRUD-A finds sanctuary and recruits among sympathetic Afar communities across the frontier. Awdal and the Somaliland question The third front confronting Djibouti is a complex border crisis along its southern frontier with Somaliland's western Awdal region. Containing the strategic coastal towns of Zeila and Lughaye, Awdal is populated by the Gadabuursi community alongside Issa communities sharing deep cross-border ties with Djibouti. The Ethiopia-Somaliland MoU elevated the geopolitical stakes in Awdal. Reports from international agencies document significant local tensions surrounding the Xeer Ciise mobilization, competing Issa and Gadabuursi clan dynamics, and political friction following Israel's formal recognition of Somaliland in December 2025. Dozens of security incidents involving clan militias were recorded across western Somaliland, highlighting how localized clan disputes can become entangled with regional port competition. Investigative reports have alleged that senior Djiboutian security officials--including Presidential Guard commander Mohamed Jama, Armed Forces commander General Zekeriye, former minister Ismail Tani, and an operative identified as Subagle--were involved in coordinating covert support to armed groups in Awdal. While Djibouti has officially rejected claims of interference, its core economic interest in preserving its port monopoly ensures that developments along the Berbera and Zeila corridors remain a top national security concern. Regional proxy competition, Houthi-Al-Shabaab nexus These border dynamics reflect a broader regional proxy competition across the Red Sea basin. On one side stands a revisionist alignment connecting Ethiopia, Somaliland, the United Arab Emirates, and Israel around commercial port development and maritime security. Opposing this alignment is a status quo coalition involving Somalia, Egypt, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia, each seeking to contain Ethiopian maritime expansion and preserve traditional diplomatic frameworks. Concurrently, illicit maritime networks across the Gulf of Aden have expanded. Reports by the United Nations Panel of Experts documented increased weapons smuggling and operational cooperation between Yemeni Houthis and Al-Shabaab in Somalia, including transfers of drone technology and explosive components. Sitting at the geographic center of these maritime corridors, Djibouti faces an extraordinary security burden in monitoring its territorial waters. Strategic importance does not confer immunity from regional instability." The human impact of this multi-front crisis is escalating. Thousands of refugees escaping escalation in Yemen have crossed the Bab el-Mandeb to Djibouti's northern coast, overwhelming reception sites like the Markazi camp. According to the latest assessments by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) , over two hundred and fifty-six thousand people--twenty-five percent of Djibouti's population--face crisis-level acute food insecurity or worse, driven by high import prices, climate shocks, and reduced humanitarian funding. President Guelleh, aged seventy-eight, has governed Djibouti since 1999. The removal of constitutional age limits enabled his continued tenure, but speculation regarding potential succession arrangements signals potential elite friction within the ruling establishment. For a country hosting major foreign bases and critical maritime infrastructure, an opaque or contested succession process poses severe risks to long-term national stability. The Dual Risk: Two fronts, one small state Djibouti's various crises are converging simultaneously on a small state apparatus whose military forces are limited in size and whose fiscal room for maneuver is constrained by debt service obligations. Deploying troops to secure the Somaliland border reduces garrison strength against FRUD insurgents in the northern districts, while focusing exclusively on domestic counter-insurgency leaves peripheral border zones vulnerable to cross-border arms trafficking. At the same time, escalating Red Sea insecurity forces foreign military bases to divert resources toward force protection, while Ethiopian port diversification directly threatens the state's primary source of foreign exchange and tax revenues. This convergence represents a triple siege--a systemic alignment of maritime, regional, and domestic pressures on a single state. Conclusion Djibouti remains an indispensable maritime actor, supported by deep-water port infrastructure, foreign military partnerships, and an irreplaceable position beside the Bab el-Mandeb. However, strategic importance does not confer immunity from regional instability. To preserve national stability, Djibouti must adapt to a changing Red Sea order. Economically, the state must diversify beyond transit rents to generate employment for its youth population. Politically, it requires institutional mechanisms capable of managing political succession and resolving long-standing Afar grievances through dialogue rather than military force alone. Regionally, it must shift from proxy competition toward pragmatic diplomatic engagement with all Red Sea neighbors. The Red Sea Cold War will not be decided solely by naval deployments or port investments but by whether littoral states can reform their domestic governance before localized grievances ignite wider regional conflicts. Djibouti remains essential to global trade and security, but its leaders must recognize that the geography that made the nation powerful can no longer shield it from the consequences of a changing regional order. Historically reliant on Ethiopia for trade, Djibouti's position is jeopardized by Ethiopia's pursuit of alternative maritime routes, particularly through Somaliland, which could diminish Djibouti's bargaining power. The ongoing Red Sea security crisis, marked by Houthi attacks, has further complicated the situation, prompting major shipping lines to reroute, impacting Djibouti's economy. The three-day gathering brought together African leaders and experts to discuss pressing security concerns, with participants emphasizing the need to address the underlying causes of instability and strengthen Africa's capacity to determine its own future. Delivering the closing address, Tana Forum Board Chairperson and President of Ghana, John Dramani Mahama, commended the outcomes of the forum and urged African leaders to translate dialogue into tangible results. "It's a good thing to talk, it's a good thing to dialogue, but it is better to act. We need to move from dialogue to action," Mahama said. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He identified the presentation of the State of Peace and Security in Africa Report as a major milestone of the forum, describing it as an important resource for assessing conflicts across the continent and developing practical responses to emerging and persistent security challenges. The Chairperson stressed that sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military deployments or standby forces alone. Instead, he called for deeper economic integration, stronger regional solidarity, expanded cross-border trade and a coordinated diplomatic approach to address the structural causes of conflict. He also underscored the importance of tackling social marginalization and building inclusive societies that create opportunities for young people, women and persons with disabilities. On governance, Mahama urged African leaders to exercise political authority in ways that improve citizens' lives, emphasizing that leadership should be measured by its contribution to public welfare rather than the possession of power itself. He further called for stronger continental unity and closer cooperation with countries of the Global South to address shared challenges and advance Africa's interests in international affairs. Reaffirming Tana Forum's role as a leading platform for high-level dialogue on African peace and security, Mahama thanked the Tana Secretariat, organizers, partners and sponsors for their contributions to the event. He also expressed appreciation to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the Ethiopian government for hosting the forum and extending hospitality to participants. The Field Marshal described both these strategic resources as vital to the country's long-term development and the well-being of future generations. Speaking at a ceremony marking the 119th anniversary of the ENDF, Field Marshal Birhanu stressed that Ethiopia must secure fair benefits from these strategic resources to sustain its prosperity and ensure future generations can benefit from the country's natural assets. He further elaborated that the Abay River as a natural resource bestowed upon Ethiopia and characterized the Red Sea as a vital resource whose benefits should serve the Ethiopian people. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He emphasized that the government and the ENDF share a responsibility to safeguard the country's national interests in both strategic water bodies. The Chief of Staff warned against what he described as attempts by a "greedy faction" to monopolize shared resources, stressing that Ethiopia would resist efforts to deny its legitimate and equitable share of the benefits. He also criticized individuals whom he accused of being misled into betraying the country's interests and aligning themselves with foreign forces, reiterating that Ethiopia would remain firm in defending its national interests. Describing the ENDF as a central pillar of the state, Field Marshal Birhanu said the force's primary responsibility is to protect Ethiopia's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national unity. He added that the military had consistently confronted external adversaries and domestic threats in carrying out its national security mandate. While underscoring Ethiopia's commitment to peaceful relations, brotherhood, and good-neighborliness with other countries, the Chief of Staff said the country would remain resolute in defending its legitimate interests. He stressed that Ethiopia's pursuit of peace and cooperation with neighboring countries would not diminish its determination to protect its national interests and ensure that its resources contribute to the prosperity of present and future generations. The annual occasion celebrates the history, traditions, and service of the Ethiopian military, reaffirming the ENDF's role in defending the nation. ethiopia.title: Endf At 119 - Advancing Ethiopia's Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Endf At 119 - Advancing Ethiopia's Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Endf At 119 - Advancing Ethiopia's Peace, Regional Stability and Tech Self-Reliance 25 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) By Staff Writer The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), marking 119 years of institutional development, represents a longstanding pillar of Ethiopia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and national security. From defending the country's independence to participating in international peacekeeping operations and expanding domestic defense manufacturing, the institution has continued to evolve in response to changing national, regional and global security demands. Today, the ENDF is pursuing a transformation that extends beyond conventional military strength. Reforms in organizational structure, professional training, technological development and defense production are intended to strengthen its operational capabilities and reduce dependence on external suppliers. At the same time, its contributions to peace and security at national, regional and international levels remain important dimensions of its institutional responsibilities. The development of the force reflects the relationship between national defense, institutional resilience and technological capacity. Its future effectiveness will depend not only on the equipment it possesses, but also on the professionalism of its personnel, the strength of its institutions and its ability to contribute to lasting peace. Resilience Legacy Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Ethiopia's military history is closely connected with its struggle to preserve independence and territorial integrity. Across successive generations, the country's armed forces have defended national sovereignty while adapting to changing political circumstances, military doctrines and technological developments. The ENDF's historical legacy includes the wider tradition of Ethiopian resistance to colonial aggression, notably the victory at Adwa in 1896, as well as the military experiences that shaped the country's subsequent defense institutions. These historical milestones preceded the establishment of the modern army and helped shape the national consciousness surrounding sovereignty and independence. Over the decades, the armed forces have undergone changes in command structures, training systems, equipment and operational responsibilities. The contemporary ENDF is building on this historical experience while seeking to develop a more professional, technologically capable and institutionally resilient force. The reform agenda pursued in recent years places particular emphasis on organizational unity, operational readiness, specialized capabilities and modern military science. In July 2026, ENDF Chief of Staff Field Marshal Birhanu Jula said the force had strengthened its unity, expanded its organizational structure and continued modernizing its equipment and technology amid an increasingly complex security environment. These efforts, he said, were intended to reinforce its capacity to safeguard Ethiopia's sovereignty. The significance of this transformation lies in its effort to connect historical experience with the requirements of contemporary national defense. A modern military must combine discipline and institutional continuity with scientific knowledge, technical expertise and the capacity to respond to rapidly changing security conditions. A Pillar of National Peace The ENDF's principal constitutional responsibility is to defend Ethiopia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Its contribution to national peace also involves protecting the country against armed threats, responding to security emergencies and supporting conditions in which citizens can pursue their social and economic activities in safety. National peace, however, extends beyond military operations. Sustainable stability requires functioning institutions, political dialogue, reconciliation, respect for the law and public confidence. The defense force can contribute to these objectives by maintaining professionalism, observing constitutional responsibilities and protecting civilians in accordance with applicable law. The ENDF's experience in complex security environments has reinforced the importance of coordination, intelligence, training and operational preparedness. Its ongoing institutional reforms seek to strengthen these capabilities while adapting to emerging threats. The force's relationship with the public is equally important. National defense is most effective when the military operates as a professional institution serving the country and its people, rather than a particular political interest. Maintaining political neutrality, respecting civilian authority and upholding the rights of citizens are essential to sustaining public trust. The military's role in national peace should therefore be assessed not only through its ability to confront armed threats, but also through its adherence to the law, protection of civilians and contribution to an environment conducive to reconciliation and development. In a country with diverse communities and complex social and political dynamics, lasting peace requires cooperation among security institutions, public authorities, communities and other stakeholders. The ENDF's professional conduct and institutional accountability are important to this broader national effort. Regional Security Ethiopia occupies a strategically important position in the Horn of Africa, a region where security developments frequently cross-national borders. The ENDF's contribution to regional peace includes cooperation with neighboring countries and participation in regional security mechanisms. Ethiopia has maintained an important role in the Eastern Africa Standby Force, an African regional arrangement designed to support peace operations and respond to crises. In May 2026, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula reaffirmed Ethiopia's commitment to regional peace and security during discussions with the outgoing and incoming leadership of the Eastern Africa Standby Force. The meeting highlighted the importance of regional cooperation in addressing shared security challenges. Such cooperation demonstrates that national defense and regional stability are interconnected. Information sharing, military coordination, joint preparedness and professional exchanges can help countries respond more effectively to threats that no single state can address independently. The ENDF's regional responsibilities must also be understood within the broader principle that durable security cannot be achieved through military measures alone. Diplomatic engagement, peaceful settlement of disputes, economic cooperation and respect for national sovereignty remain essential to preventing conflicts and strengthening relations among neighboring countries. A stable Horn of Africa would create greater opportunities for regional trade, infrastructure development, investment and economic integration. By contributing to legitimate regional security arrangements and supporting cooperative approaches to shared threats, Ethiopia's defense institutions can help create conditions for these wider development objectives. International Peacekeeping One of the most visible expressions of Ethiopia's contribution to international peace has been its participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. Ethiopian personnel have served in international missions for decades, reflecting the country's longstanding engagement with multilateral efforts to maintain peace and protect communities affected by conflict. According to the United Nations, Ethiopia's participation in UN-authorized operations dates back to 1951, when Ethiopian personnel served as part of the multinational force in the Korean War. Since then, Ethiopian military personnel have contributed to peace and security operations in different parts of the world. A prominent example is the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA), established in 2011 to help stabilize the disputed Abyei area between Sudan and South Sudan. The mission monitors security arrangements, supports the protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, and contributes to efforts to prevent renewed violence. The deployment of Ethiopian troops to Abyei followed an agreement reached by Sudanese and South Sudanese representatives in Addis Ababa. The mission illustrates how Ethiopian military personnel have supported internationally mandated security arrangements in a sensitive border region. Ethiopian personnel have also served in other United Nations missions, including operations in South Sudan. Their responsibilities have included supporting civilian protection, maintaining security in designated areas and helping create conditions for humanitarian activities and political processes. These experiences have given Ethiopian peacekeepers opportunities to work within multinational command structures, cooperate with personnel from different countries and apply international peacekeeping standards in demanding operational environments. International peacekeeping also strengthens professional experience. Service in multinational missions exposes military personnel to different approaches to logistics, communication, civilian protection and operational coordination. Lessons gained from these assignments can contribute to training and institutional development at home. The broader significance of Ethiopia's peacekeeping record is that military capability can serve purposes beyond national defense. When deployed under an authorized mandate and in accordance with international law, disciplined military personnel can help protect vulnerable populations, support humanitarian access and contribute to efforts to restore stability. Defense Technology, Industrial Capacity Alongside its peace and security responsibilities, the ENDF is pursuing a transformation in military technology and domestic production. The objective is to strengthen the country's ability to manufacture, maintain and sustain essential defense equipment while developing the technical expertise required for modern military operations. For a country with extensive security responsibilities, dependence on foreign suppliers can affect the availability, maintenance and long-term sustainability of military equipment. Developing domestic production capacity can help reduce these vulnerabilities, retain technical knowledge and build a stronger industrial foundation for national defense. Ethiopia's defense industrial institutions provide important examples of this approach. The Homicho Ammunition Engineering Complex is associated with domestic ammunition production, while the wider defense industry has been working to strengthen capabilities in equipment manufacturing, engineering and maintenance. These facilities illustrate how defense production can bring together mechanical engineering, industrial processes, technical training and specialized manufacturing. Their strategic importance lies not simply in the products they manufacture, but also in the knowledge and skills developed through sustained industrial activity. Developing domestic expertise in this field can also expand opportunities for engineering research and technical education. Another significant step came in June 2026, when the Information Network Security Administration and the Ethiopian Air Force signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a drone technology center and strengthen research, laboratory cooperation and aerospace capabilities. The initiative is intended to support innovation and the development of local expertise in unmanned aerial systems. In August 2026, the ENDF and the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute also signed a cooperation agreement to explore the application of artificial intelligence in areas including logistics, military training, cybersecurity, military healthcare, air operations and electronic warfare. The agreement points to a broader shift in defense modernization. Military effectiveness increasingly depends on the ability to collect, process and use information, maintain secure communications and support rapid, informed decision-making. Artificial intelligence and related digital technologies could contribute to these objectives, although their operational benefits will depend on research, testing, qualified personnel and effective implementation. These initiatives demonstrate that Ethiopia's defense transformation is not limited to acquiring modern equipment. It also involves building the scientific, industrial and educational capabilities required to develop and sustain advanced systems. Human Capital Dimension Technology alone cannot create an effective defense institution. Modern military systems require skilled operators, engineers, technicians, researchers, maintenance specialists and commanders capable of applying scientific knowledge to operational requirements. For this reason, investment in military education and professional development is central to the ENDF's modernization. Military academies, specialized training institutions and cooperation with civilian research organizations can help develop the expertise needed to operate sophisticated equipment and maintain complex systems. The partnership between the ENDF, the Ethiopian Air Force, the Information Network Security Administration and the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute illustrates the potential value of cooperation between defense institutions and the wider scientific community. Such partnerships can strengthen research capacity, encourage the exchange of technical knowledge and support the development of locally relevant solutions. They can also help cultivate a generation of Ethiopian engineers and researchers whose expertise may contribute to defense manufacturing and other technology-intensive sectors. Domestic defense production can generate benefits beyond the military when it develops transferable industrial skills, strengthens engineering capacity and encourages research and innovation. The long-term objective is to build a system in which training, research, manufacturing and operational requirements reinforce one another. This would enable Ethiopia to develop more of the expertise necessary to maintain its defense capabilities while creating a stronger foundation for technological advancement. Self-Reliance The ENDF's industrial and technological transformation forms part of Ethiopia's wider pursuit of productive capacity and economic self-reliance. Similar priorities are evident in the country's efforts to expand agricultural production, develop mineral resources, strengthen manufacturing and invest in scientific knowledge. Nevertheless, it can contribute to broader industrial development by encouraging specialized engineering, technical training and domestic manufacturing. The development of ammunition production, engineering facilities and drone research demonstrates the range of capabilities required to build a more self-reliant defense sector. These initiatives can help strengthen maintenance capacity, improve the availability of selected equipment and create opportunities for domestic technical expertise. It is important, however, to distinguish progress in selected areas from complete self-sufficiency. Modern military systems depend on extensive supply chains involving specialized components, software, materials and technical knowledge. Building sustainable domestic capacity is therefore a continuing process that requires investment, research, reliable production standards and international technical cooperation where necessary. The strongest measure of progress is not the number of factories established or the equipment acquired, but the ability to produce reliable systems, maintain them over time, develop skilled personnel and meet clearly identified national defense requirements. Its responsibilities remain broad: protecting national sovereignty, contributing to domestic security within the law, supporting regional stability and participating in international peacekeeping. Meeting these responsibilities requires an institution that is well trained, technically capable, disciplined and accountable. The development of domestic defense industries, drone technology and artificial intelligence cooperation indicates a growing emphasis on technological preparedness. Sustaining these efforts will require stronger research institutions, skilled human resources, effective industrial management and continued adaptation to changing military technologies. Equally important is the relationship between security and peace. Military readiness can deter threats and help protect communities, but lasting stability also depends on dialogue, diplomacy, reconciliation and cooperation among nations and communities. The ENDF's long-term contribution will be strengthened when professional defense capabilities complement these wider efforts. The force's 119-year institutional journey thus represents both a historical legacy and a continuing responsibility. Its achievements in national defense, regional cooperation, international peacekeeping and technological development provide a foundation on which further progress can be built. Ultimately, the strength of the Ethiopian National Defense Force will be measured not only by its capacity to defend the country, but also by its professionalism, its contribution to a secure regional environment and its ability to adapt responsibly to the demands of modern defense. France24 The United Nations (UN) has announced plans to end its transitional mission in Somalia after more than three decades of involvement in the country's peacebuilding efforts, even as the threat of Al-Shabaab attacks persists along Kenya's border. In a statement issued on Monday, October 26, UN Secretary-General António Guterres confirmed that the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) would officially cease operations on October 31, 2026. The decision follows resolutions adopted by the UN Security Council in 2024 and 2025, alongside a request by Somalia's federal government to transfer greater responsibility for the country's political and security affairs to its own institutions. According to the UN, the mission's responsibilities have already been transferred to Somali institutions and other UN agencies, ending a period of international involvement in peacebuilding, governance and reconciliation that began more than 30 years ago. An undated image of United Nation's Headquarters in New York, US. Photo UN However, Guterres acknowledged that Somalia continues to face significant security challenges, particularly the threat posed by Al-Shabaab, and called for continued international support to prevent the country from losing gains made over the years . The development comes as Kenya continues to experience attacks linked to the militant group, particularly in Mandera County, where security officers have repeatedly confronted suspected Al-Shabaab fighters operating near the Kenya-Somalia border. On September 6, Kenyan security personnel reportedly repelled an attack by suspected Al-Shabaab militants in Arabia Town, Mandera County, following a nighttime assault that triggered hours of gunfire between the attackers and security forces. The incident followed several other attacks reported in the county, including one near Wantey Dam on July 28 and 29, which left five Special Operations Group officers dead. A vehicle carrying reinforcements was also reportedly targeted by an explosive device. Earlier, on July 25, police reportedly foiled coordinated attacks targeting Fino camp and Arabia village, while a separate operation on July 13 resulted in the deaths of 11 suspected militants accused of planning an assault on a nearby village. The persistent insecurity has also complicated plans to reopen the Kenya-Somalia border, which has remained officially closed for more than 13 years, with President William Ruto previously citing security concerns despite repeated commitments to restore cross-border movement. Kenya has also maintained a military presence in Somalia since 2011, when its troops entered the country under Operation Linda Nchi before joining African Union-led security operations against Al-Shabaab. However, the closure of UNTMIS does not affect the separate African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which includes Kenyan troops and whose current mandate is set to expire on December 31, 2026, unless extended. The man had been placed in isolation after health authorities determined that he had direct contact with a person infected with Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease who later died in Kenya. advertisements “Following up on the statement issued on October 12, 2026, the Ministry shares with the Somali public the latest information regarding the Somali citizen who was placed under quarantine,” the Health Ministry said. The ministry said the man was transferred on Oct. 12 to an Ebola quarantine and treatment center at Forlanini Hospital in Mogadishu, where he was monitored under infection-control protocols. He underwent two Ebola tests, one conducted in Somalia and another sent abroad for confirmation. Both returned negative, the ministry said. The man also remained free of Ebola symptoms throughout the quarantine period and completed 21 days of monitoring, the maximum incubation period generally used for Ebola contact follow-up. “Taking into account the results of both tests, the completion of the monitoring period, the citizen’s health status, and an assessment of public health risks ... the Ministry of Health has decided to release the citizen from quarantine,” the statement said. Somalia’s Health Ministry also stressed that no Ebola cases have been confirmed in the country. Health Minister Dr. Ali Haji Adan said authorities would continue surveillance and monitoring as the regional outbreak develops. The exposure was linked to Kenya’s first confirmed case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, an imported case involving a man who had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on Oct. 3. He tested positive on Oct. 5 and died later that day, according to the World Health Organization. Kenyan authorities initially identified dozens of contacts connected to the case and placed high-risk contacts under quarantine. By Oct. 20, Kenya had reported nine Bundibugyo Ebola cases, including deaths, all linked to the original imported case, according to WHO. Somali health authorities have not reported any locally acquired or imported confirmed Ebola infection.
