Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali Plundering the Seas: How Corruption and Secret Foreign Deals Dismantled Somalia’s Blue Economy Staff Reporter GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 27-10-2026, 06:48AM MOGADISHU, Somalia — When delegates gathered in Mogadishu today for the opening of the 3rd Somali Fisheries Week, the atmosphere inside the venue bore little resemblance to the ambitious national vision once promised to the Somali public. What was officially advertised as a premier week-long international summit celebrating the nation’s vast maritime potential laid bare severe institutional decay, systemic financial misappropriation, and the systematic surrender of Somalia's marine sovereign rights to foreign actors? Despite its grand title, today’s gathering was abruptly compressed into a hasty two-day event, stripped of the multilateral backing, donor confidence, and broad institutional participation that defined previous iterations. The fall of Somali Fisheries Week The contrast between today’s scaled-back gathering and earlier editions could not be more glaring: · Inaugurated with high expectations in September 2024, the inaugural Somali Fisheries Week was an authentic, multi-day national exhibition. It brought together over ten major international donor partners, development agencies, local fishing cooperatives, and regional government delegations aimed at leveraging Somalia’s 3,300\text{ km} coastline for sustainable local development. · Monday’s gathering lasted mere hours. Deprived of international legitimacy and abandoned by legitimate sector stakeholders, the rebranded "week" functioned as little more than a staged political photo opportunity, underscoring the deep isolation into which the ministry’s current leadership has driven the sector. Financial Mismanagement and Donor Flight At the heart of this institutional collapse lies the fallout from the September 2024 edition of Somali Fisheries Week. Subsequent investigations and financial reviews revealed widespread irregularities and misappropriation of funds allocated by international development agencies for sector reform and coastal development. Following these severe financial breaches, primary Western development partners—most notably the United States (USAID) and the United Kingdom (FCDO)—completely withdrew their funding commitments for the 2025 and 2026 fisheries programs. The exit of key international backers sent shockwaves through the Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy, instantly cutting off critical technical assistance, anti-piracy monitoring support, and coastal livelihood grants designed for local fishing communities. Foreign Lifelines and Sovereign Concessions Facing an acute budgetary crisis brought on by donor flight, Minister Ahmed Hassan Adan and Director General Abdi Dirshe bypassed standard parliamentary oversight, procurement laws, and constitutional checks to secure operational funding elsewhere. The Turkish Fisheries Deal To replace lost Western donor funds, Ministry leadership finalized a controversial, multimillion-dollar fisheries arrangement with representatives from Ankara, brokered directly through the Turkish Embassy in Mogadishu. Under the guise of bilateral economic cooperation, the agreement effectively opens Somalia’s rich Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) to foreign industrial commercial fleets. Maritime legal experts, civil society organizations, and local coastal advocacy groups have condemned the transaction, asserting that the Minister and Director General have signed away Somalia’s irreplaceable marine resources in exchange for short-term financial bailouts to cover ministry shortfalls. Unlawful Regulatory Delegations via Hope Labs Group Compounding the governance scandal is the improper involvement of Hope Labs Group. The private company was quietly contracted by the ministry to oversee key regulatory affairs, licensing mechanisms, and maritime compliance frameworks without fulfilling standard public bidding, statutory approvals, or legal vetting procedures. By handing over critical sovereign regulatory powers to an unvented private entity, the leadership of the Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy has subverted public oversight. This opaque arrangement leaves local artisanal fishers vulnerable to unchecked industrial exploitation, ecosystem degradation, and unregulated foreign competition across Somali waters. A Sector at a Crossroads The 3rd Somali Fisheries Week stands as a stark warning of how crucial national developmental initiatives can be reduced to optics to mask administrative malfeasance. While ministry leadership celebrates short-term foreign funding injections, local coastal communities face declining fish stocks, environmental damage, and escalating economic displacement. Without immediate parliamentary scrutiny, independent anti-corruption investigations, and a thorough audit of the bilateral agreements signed by Minister Ahmed Hassan Adan and Director General Abdi Dirshe, Somalia risks permanently surrendering the economic sovereign rights of its greatest natural asset—its ocean. File Photo | AP AFP Updated on : 27 Oct 2026, 6:27 am 1 min read Copied MOGADISHU: Islamist insurgent group Al-Shabaab claimed to have killed hundreds of Somali government troops in an ambush on Monday. The Al-Qaeda-linked group has been fighting the government for two decades and still controls large swathes of central Somalia despite a massive international operation against it. According to the SITE Intelligence Group, Al-Shabaab issued a statement late Monday saying it had launched an attack on Turkish-trained government troops and an allied militia -- supported by Turkish fighter jets -- in the Lower Shabelle region, resulting in the deaths of 321 troops. The toll could not be independently verified, and the government did not immediately offer a response. The fighting, near the city of Leego, continued for three hours and resulted in the seizure of prisoners, weapons and vehicles, according to Al-Shabaab's statement. Local media platform Baidoa Online said the government had called an emergency meeting of the cabinet to discuss the "heavy casualties and substantial military equipment losses during intense fighting with Al-Shabaab militants near Leego". Turkey has emerged as a key backer of the Somali government at a time when the United States and other key donors are pulling back from supporting the counter-insurgency. Washington has stopped funding the vital United Nations logistics mission that supplies combat operations in the country, saying the government has failed to make progress in uniting the country and tackling the insurgent threat. somalia.content: UN mission in Somalia ends October 31 after successful two-year transition For You News Faida Cafe Shows Radio TV Podcasts Live Events Search UN mission in Somalia ends October 31 after successful two-year transition By Teddy Eugene Otieno October 27, 2026 08:49 (EAT) Add as a Preferred Source on Google Follow us Follow on Whatsapp Follow on Google Follow on Twitter Audio By Vocalize The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will cease operations on October 31, marking the end of a two-year transition process and bringing to a close more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding and state-building in the Horn of Africa. According to a statement issued by UN Secretary-General António Guterres’ spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric, the mission’s closure follows Security Council resolutions 2753 (2024) and 2809 (2025), as well as a request by the Federal Government of Somalia. The transition was guided by a roadmap jointly agreed upon by the Somali government and the United Nations. Under the arrangement, UNTMIS’s mandated functions have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, funds and programmes. The move is intended to strengthen national ownership of Somalia’s peacebuilding, governance and state-building agenda, with Somali institutions assuming greater responsibility for the country’s development and reconciliation efforts. Guterres commended the progress made over the past decades in advancing peace and security in Somalia, praising the determination and resilience of its people despite persistent challenges. He said the United Nations would continue supporting Somalia through its resident agencies, funds and programmes, working with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners to promote peace, stability, human rights and sustainable development. However, the UN chief warned that significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges remain. He called for sustained international support to consolidate the gains made, promote inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions and protect human rights. Guterres also underscored the need for continued assistance to counter the threat posed by Al-Shabaab and support a gradual and sustainable transition in the country’s security arrangements. The Secretary-General expressed gratitude to successive UN special representatives and national and international personnel who served in UNTMIS and its predecessor missions, acknowledging their contribution to peace and state-building efforts under difficult conditions. He also paid tribute to UN personnel who lost their lives while serving in Somalia. somalia.content: Somali President defends direct elections, invites opposition to talks amid electoral dispute - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somali President defends direct elections, invites opposition to talks amid electoral dispute Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 27, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud defended his government’s push for one-person, one-vote elections in a televised address Sunday, while renewing an invitation to opposition leaders for talks aimed at resolving a widening dispute over the country’s electoral process. Mohamud described direct voting as the beginning of Somalia’s return to a democratic system after decades of indirect elections, but acknowledged that the country’s political process had not yet reached its intended destination. advertisements “Although Somalia has navigated various political phases over the past 30 years, an opportunity now exists to strengthen a system in which the public directly elects its leaders,” Mohamud said. Somalia has largely relied since 2000 on indirect elections in which clan delegates select lawmakers, who in turn elect the president. Mohamud argued that recent local and regional voting represented progress toward restoring universal suffrage. The president said direct elections had taken place in parts of South West, Galmudug and Hirshabelle states and in the Banadir region, covering 50 of the 92 districts that existed in 1990. According to figures presented by Mohamud, 1,824,853 people registered to vote at 1,102 polling stations. He said 26,742 candidates contested the elections and 1,435 officials were elected through direct voting. Those figures were presented by the president and were not independently verified in his address. Mohamud also maintained that voting took place without armed confrontations at polling stations and that electoral authorities complied with the law and Supreme Court rulings. “Not a single armed incident occurred at any polling station across the country, and the rule of law was upheld through compliance with the Supreme Court’s rulings,” he said. The president praised former officials and political figures who accepted election results despite disagreements over the process. “Respecting the will of the people and accepting the results are the foundation of a lasting democracy,” Mohamud said. His remarks come amid a deepening dispute between the federal government, opposition groups and some federal member states over constitutional amendments, the electoral framework and the mandates of federal institutions. Somalia’s National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission announced earlier this month that elections for both houses of the federal parliament would be held on April 15, 2027, followed by a presidential election on May 15. Opposition groups have rejected the timetable, arguing that it was announced without an inclusive political agreement. Puntland, Jubaland and several opposition figures have also challenged aspects of the revised constitutional framework and called for negotiations before the federal elections proceed. Mohamud used Sunday’s address to insist that political disagreements should be resolved through dialogue, consensus and compromise rather than confrontation. He formally called on political leaders to return to negotiations through official channels and urged opposition figures and community leaders to avoid actions that could threaten national stability. The president also clarified earlier remarks in which he had argued that national decisions could not remain indefinitely unresolved. He said he was not rejecting consultation but drawing a distinction between consultation and the eventual need to make decisions. On Monday, the presidency followed the address by inviting the Nabad iyo Nolol Party, the Somali Future Council, the National Unity Forum and a civil society coalition to a national consultative forum in Mogadishu from Nov. 14 to 18. The talks are expected to focus on reaching common ground over federal election arrangements. The Somali Future Council, which includes opposition figures and the Puntland and Jubaland administrations, has previously expressed willingness to resume substantive negotiations while demanding what it describes as a realistic and mutually agreed electoral timetable. Mohamud also reiterated his government’s commitment to continuing military operations against al-Shabab, strengthening national security and completing the transition toward direct elections. “Our objective is to ensure that the Somali people enjoy their right to elect their leaders through their votes,” Mohamud said. Whether the latest invitation leads to an electoral agreement remains uncertain. Previous government-opposition negotiations have failed to resolve disputes over the electoral model, management of the vote and the role of federal member states. somalia.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Mark Townsend in Kismayo Tuesday October 27, 2026 Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy? A colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023. Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Images The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river. “The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.” Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba. advertisements “The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.” Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets. The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians. The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital. Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month. An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia. Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead. “The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source. When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm. Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.” US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.” Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño. Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.” Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater. “In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old. US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”. Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000. Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half. His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba. Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says. The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled. Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient. “They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks. Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”. Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets. Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said. Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.” Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter. “It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.” Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided. Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes. Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region. Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year. David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.” The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.” Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia. Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them. Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart. Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.” In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea. El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine. Fadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year. Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night. For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness. “She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived. Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse. As El Niño intensifies the rainy season, residents in areas like Jilib report constant airstrikes that have devastated their communities and left them with no safe refuge. Eyewitness accounts describe significant civilian casualties, with many bodies left in the streets. Critics argue that the US military strategy appears to exploit the flooding to weaken al-Shabaab, the militant group controlling much of the region. Although US officials deny targeting civilians or using weather as a weapon, the situation raises ethical concerns about the military's operations and the potential for large-scale humanitarian crises. With inadequate flood defenses and dwindling resources, the looming threat of severe flooding exacerbates the already dire conditions for those living in al-Shabaab territory, where hunger and displacement are rampant.

football.title: الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا - شبكة مصدر الاخبارية
football.content: الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا - شبكة مصدر الاخبارية الرئيسية فلسطينيو 48 شؤون إسرائيلية عربية وإقليمية اقتصاد تكنولوجيا تقارير خاصة رياضة منوعات إتصل بنا الرئيسية رياضة الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا نواذيبو الموريتاني يعوض خسارة الذهاب ويبلغ الدور المقبل.. وقرعة المجموعات تُجرى الأربعاء المقبل الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا 26 أكتوبر 2026 12:00 ص وكالات - واصل الأفريقي التونسي مشواره في دوري أبطال أفريقيا لكرة القدم، بعدما حجز بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات بفوزه على ضيفه تي بي مازيمبي، بطل الكونغو الديمقراطية، بهدف دون رد، الأحد، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني للمسابقة. وسجل الكاميروني تاديوس نكينغ هدف المباراة الوحيد في الدقيقة الثانية من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط الأول، ليمنح الفريق التونسي انتصاراً ثميناً على أرضه، بعد مواجهة اتسمت بأهمية كبيرة للطرفين. وكانت مباراة الذهاب، التي أُقيمت في مدينة لومومباشي الكونغولية الأسبوع الماضي، قد انتهت بالتعادل 1-1، ليحسم الأفريقي التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 2-1. وبهذا الإنجاز، أصبح الأفريقي الممثل الثاني للكرة التونسية في مرحلة المجموعات هذا الموسم، إلى جانب غريمه التقليدي الترجي التونسي، فيما تبخرت آمال مازيمبي في مواصلة مشواره نحو اللقب السادس في تاريخه، والأول منذ عام 2015. ويطمح الأفريقي إلى استعادة أمجاده القارية والمنافسة على لقبه الثاني في البطولة، بعدما سبق له التتويج بدوري أبطال أفريقيا عام 1991. نواذيبو الموريتاني يقلب تأخره ويعبر إلى المرحلة الرئيسية وفي العاصمة الموريتانية نواكشوط، انتزع نواذيبو بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما تغلب على ضيفه سان بيدرو الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-0، على ملعب «شيخ ولد بيديا»، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني. وبدأ الفريق الموريتاني المواجهة بقوة، وافتتح كارتييه ديمبيلي التسجيل في الدقيقة العاشرة، ليمنح أصحاب الأرض تقدماً مبكراً أعاد المواجهة إلى نقطة التعادل في مجموع المباراتين. وفي الدقيقة 53، أضاف شيخ خطاب الهدف الثاني لنواذيبو، ليعزز فرص فريقه في حسم بطاقة التأهل ويمنحه الأفضلية اللازمة بعد خسارة مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 2-1 خارج أرضه. وبهذا الفوز، عوض نواذيبو خسارته في اللقاء الأول، ليتفوق بنتيجة 3-2 في مجموع المباراتين، ويواصل حضوره في المنافسات القارية، بعدما نجح في استثمار عاملي الأرض والجمهور لحسم المواجهة. ويمثل التأهل خطوة مهمة للنادي الموريتاني، الذي نجح في تجاوز عقبة منافس إيفواري بعد مواجهة امتدت حساباتها إلى المباراتين، ليحجز مكانه بين أندية مرحلة المجموعات. المغرب الفاسي يحسم التأهل بهدف قاتل في أبيدجان بدوره، تأهل المغرب الفاسي إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما حقق فوزاً ثميناً على أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-1 في العاصمة أبيدجان، مستفيداً من تعادله في مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 1-1 في مكناس. وبعد انتهاء الشوط الأول بالتعادل السلبي، افتتح الكونغولي كريستوفر إيبايي التسجيل للمغرب الفاسي، قبل أن يتمكن كيفين باكارا من إدراك التعادل لأسيك ميموزا، لتزداد صعوبة المواجهة مع اقتراب نهايتها. وبينما كانت المباراة تتجه إلى ركلات الترجيح، خطف خالد بابا هدف الفوز للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع، ليمنح فريقه انتصاراً خارج أرضه بنتيجة 2-1 ويحسم تأهله. وجاء الهدف المتأخر ليضع حداً لمواجهة قوية بين الفريقين، ويمنح النادي المغربي بطاقة العبور بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 3-2. ولحق المغرب الفاسي بمواطنه نهضة بركان، وصيف البطولة، الذي ضمن بدوره التأهل بعد إقصاء ستار سبورت أكاديمي السيراليوني، بالفوز عليه ذهاباً وإياباً. ويعزز تأهل الفريقين الحضور المغربي في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، بعدما نجحا في تجاوز منافسيهما في الدور التمهيدي الثاني. الهلال السوداني يكرر فوزه على سيداما بونا وفي العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، التي يتخذها الهلال السوداني ملعباً بيتياً، كرر الفريق فوزه على ضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليحجز مقعده في مرحلة المجموعات. وكان الهلال قد فاز بالنتيجة نفسها في مباراة الذهاب، ليحسم التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 4-0، مؤكداً تفوقه على منافسه في المواجهتين. وجاءت ثنائية الفريق السوداني في الشوط الأول، إذ افتتح إرنست لوزولو التسجيل في الدقيقة 33، قبل أن يضيف محمد عبد الرحمن «الغربال» الهدف الثاني في الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط. ومنح الانتصار الهلال فرصة مواصلة مشواره القاري، كما عوض جماهيره جزئياً عن خروج غريمه التقليدي المريخ من المسابقة، بعدما ودع البطولة السبت على يد حوريا الغيني بركلات الترجيح. وبهذا التأهل، يواصل الهلال تمثيل الكرة السودانية في البطولة، وسط تطلعات إلى تقديم أداء قوي في مرحلة المجموعات والمنافسة على بلوغ الأدوار الإقصائية. سيمبا وكولوم يكملان قائمة المتأهلين وشهدت بقية مباريات الدور التمهيدي الثاني تأهل سيمبا التنزاني، بعدما حقق فوزاً عريضاً على فريق 15 أوغوستو القادم من غينيا الاستوائية بنتيجة 3-0. وجاء الانتصار ليمنح سيمبا تفوقاً كبيراً في مجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 9-1، بعدما كان قد حقق نتيجة إيجابية في لقاء الذهاب، ليعبر إلى المرحلة المقبلة بأفضلية واضحة. كما تأهل كولومب الكاميروني إلى مرحلة المجموعات، عقب فوزه على تينغيت السنغالي بهدف دون رد في مباراة الإياب، مستفيداً من انتصاره في لقاء الذهاب بنتيجة 2-0، ليحسم المواجهة بمجموع 3-0. وتعكس هذه النتائج اتساع رقعة المنافسة بين أندية القارة، مع نجاح فرق من تونس وموريتانيا والمغرب والسودان وتنزانيا والكاميرون في حجز مقاعدها بالمرحلة الرئيسية من البطولة. قرعة المجموعات الأربعاء المقبل تتجه أنظار الأندية المتأهلة إلى قرعة مرحلة المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، المقرر إجراؤها الأربعاء المقبل، حيث ستتحدد مواجهات المرحلة المقبلة ومسارات المنافسة نحو الأدوار الإقصائية. وتكتسب القرعة أهمية كبيرة بالنسبة إلى الفرق التي تجاوزت football.summary: حسم الهلال السوداني تأهله إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد فوزه على سيداما كوفي الإثيوبي بهدفين دون رد في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني، ليحقق مجموع 4-0 في مباراتي الذهاب والإياب. وقد أظهر الهلال أداءً قويًا خلال المباراتين، مما يعكس استعداده الجيد للمنافسات المقبلة. في المقابل، تمكن المغرب الفاسي من خطف بطاقة التأهل في مباراة مثيرة ضد أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري، حيث انتهت المباراة بفوز المغرب الفاسي 2-1. سجل كريستوفر إيباي هدف التقدم للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة 62، لكن أسيك ميموزا أدرك التعادل في الدقيقة 73. ومع ذلك، سجل خالد بابا هدف الانتصار القاتل في الدقيقة 97، ليقود فريقه إلى التأهل بمجموع 3-2. هذه النتائج تعكس تنافسية البطولة وتوقعات مثيرة للجولات القادمة.
